hypothesis.title: The Translation Loss
hypothesis.question: Which musical layer must a representation preserve for a transformed passage to still be heard as the same music?
hypothesis.hypothesis: If a musical identity is carried by a layer that a translation weakens, then listeners will report reduced coherence or identity even when surface audio quality remains acceptable.
hypothesis.rationaleMd: The selected sources suggest that representations preserve task-specific layers rather than whole musical objects. Ice phases depend on accessible transition paths rather than abstract possibility space [S1]. Bark-scale dynamics treats frequency resolution as perceptual rather than arbitrary [S2]. StreamMark survives benign acoustic transformations but fails under semantics-altering attacks, separating surface preservation from identity preservation [S3]. PHALAR's phase-equivariant representation improves stem retrieval and aligns better with human coherence judgments, implying that phase can carry musical relatedness [S4]. MSU-Bench shows that score modality changes multilevel musical reasoning [S5], while speech-recognition fairness work identifies the audio encoder, not language-model scale, as the decisive layer for robustness and bias [S6].

recipe.title: Load-Bearing Layer Litmus
recipe.bodyMd: Compose a 60-second miniature with a clear melodic identity, a repeated rhythmic cell, and a recognizable timbral carrier. Export three translations. Version A preserves pitch and rhythm but weakens phase-sensitive microtiming with magnitude-heavy spectral resynthesis, testing the PHALAR claim that phase contributes to coherence [S4]. Version B preserves timing but applies 24-band Bark-style dynamics so each perceptual band breathes independently, testing whether perceptual frequency banding changes identity without destroying audio quality [S2]. Version C preserves notation-level pitch/rhythm while changing carriers and inserting brief rests/silence masks, testing score-modality and encoder-fragility questions raised by MSU-Bench and speech-recognition degradation work [S5][S6]. Compare against an unprocessed reference. The hypothesis is supported if one transformation has acceptable surface quality but clearly loses same-piece identity; it is weakened if all transformations preserve identity equally or all fail only because of obvious audio degradation. StreamMark provides the analogy: robustness to benign surface change is not the same thing as robustness to meaning-changing transformation [S3].

parameters.value: SNR target near 24.16 dB for hidden-layer processing audibility check

dawChecklist: Write one 60-second reference miniature with melody, rhythm, harmony, and a distinctive timbral carrier.
Export the dry reference and loudness-match all later renders.
Create Version A with spectral processing that preserves pitch contour but reduces phase/microtiming detail.
Create Version B with 24-band Bark-style dynamics or the closest available critical-band multiband setup.
Create Version C by preserving score-level pitch/rhythm while changing instruments and inserting short rests or silence masks.
Blind-label the four files and rate same-piece identity, coherence, timbral continuity, and surface audio quality.
Mark the load-bearing layer as the lowest-level feature whose damage reduces identity while surface quality remains acceptable.

protocol.listeningContext: Nearfield monitoring or headphones at matched loudness.
protocol.listeningMethod: Blind A/B/C/reference comparison with written ratings immediately after each pass.
whatVaries: representation layer damaged: phase/microtiming, perceptual band dynamics, timbral carrier/rest masking
